lesson.menu_title: The Invitation to Boston -- Reading an International Agenda

lesson.subtitle: Lesson 10 -- The Invitation to Boston
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Renato Annunciato | Lesson 10 -- The Invitation to Boston

listenings.text: I have been going to these global meetings for about twelve years, and the first thing I tell people is that the agenda is not the meeting. The sessions are useful, and the keynote is usually good, but the conversations that change something happen in the twenty minutes between them. That is when you meet the person who signs off on your budget, or the colleague in another country who has already solved the problem you are stuck on. So my advice is simple. Read the delegate list before you fly. Choose three people you want to speak to, and find out one real thing about their market. Then, when you are on site, do not have lunch with your own country team every day. You already know them. Sit somewhere else. And one last thing, about English. Nobody at these meetings speaks perfect English, and nobody cares. What people remember is whether you had something to say about your own market. Prepare two sentences about yours and you will be fine.

I organise four of these meetings a year, and delegates forget the same three things every time. The first is the confirmation. The invitation asks you to confirm attendance by a date, and that date is not decoration. Rooms are booked from that number, and the airport transfers are arranged from that number too. If you confirm late you will still come, but you may be put in a hotel twenty minutes away from everybody else. The second is the badge. It is collected on site, at the desk, on the first morning, and it is needed for every room in the building. People arrive at nine, walk straight to the first session, and are stopped at the door. And the third is the breakout. Delegates read the keynote and the plenary sessions carefully, and then they ignore the breakouts, which is exactly where they are expected to speak. If your name is printed next to a breakout, you are not the audience. You are part of it.

extra_audio.text: Thank you for the invitation to the Global Commercial Meeting in Boston. I am writing to confirm my attendance on both days. Could you confirm which breakout I am expected to take part in? I would be happy to present the results from the South and Southeast of Brazil.

paras: The Global Commercial Meeting will be held in Boston on the fourteenth and fifteenth of March. All country commercial managers are invited, and around ninety delegates are expected from twenty-two markets. The meeting is hosted by the Global Commercial team, and the venue is the conference centre on the harbour, ten minutes from the main hotel.

A full itinerary was sent with this invitation. Attendance must be confirmed by the tenth of February, because rooms and airport transfers are booked from the confirmed list. A shuttle is provided between the hotel and the venue every thirty minutes on both mornings. Badges are collected on site, at the registration desk, from seven thirty on the first day, and they are needed for every room in the building.

The first morning is opened by a keynote from the Global Head of Commercial. The rest of day one is organised into plenary sessions, and day two is given to breakouts, where each region is asked to present in a small group. Managers who are invited to a breakout are informed by the end of January.

Delegates are asked to bring one slide on the biggest opportunity in their market. The slides are collected in advance and are printed for the room, so nothing is presented from a laptop. Questions about visas, travel or accommodation should be sent to Global Events, and they are usually answered within two working days.
